scenes.headline: South Africa's biggest corporate collapses
scenes.body: Banks, retailers, airlines and one crypto scheme. Counted down from ten to one.
scenes.voiceover: Billions of rand, gone. Deposits, pensions and jobs, wiped out. These are the ten biggest corporate collapses in South African history, counted down from ten to one.

scenes.headline: Money lost, people hurt, rules changed.
scenes.body: The higher on the list, the wider the damage and the longer the fallout.
scenes.voiceover: We ranked them on three things. How much money was lost, how many ordinary people were hurt, and how much each collapse changed the rules afterwards.

scenes.headline: LeisureNet
scenes.voiceover: Number ten. LeisureNet.

scenes.name: LeisureNet
scenes.headline: The gym empire that ran out of cash
scenes.body: Owner of Health and Racquet Clubs. Liquidated, with its founders later convicted of fraud.
scenes.voiceover: LeisureNet owned the Health and Racquet Club gyms and expanded fast, including overseas. In two thousand it collapsed into liquidation, and its founders were later convicted of fraud.

scenes.headline: Comair
scenes.voiceover: Number nine. Comair.

scenes.name: Comair
scenes.headline: kulula.com and BA's local flights, grounded
scenes.body: Covid-era losses it never recovered from. Thousands of jobs gone overnight.
scenes.voiceover: Comair ran kulula dot com and British Airways flights in South Africa. After the pandemic years it never recovered, and in twenty twenty-two the planes stopped flying for good.

scenes.headline: Edcon
scenes.voiceover: Number eight. Edcon.

scenes.name: Edcon
scenes.headline: Edgars and Jet, sold off piece by piece
scenes.body: Years of debt, then lockdown. The group entered business rescue and its brands were sold.
scenes.voiceover: Edcon owned Edgars and Jet, household names for generations. Heavy debt had weakened it for years, and when lockdown closed its stores in twenty twenty, it went into business rescue. Its brands were sold off to other retailers.

scenes.headline: South African Airways
scenes.voiceover: Number seven. South African Airways.

scenes.name: SAA
scenes.headline: Bailout after bailout, paid by taxpayers
scenes.body: The national carrier needed repeated state rescues before entering business rescue.
scenes.voiceover: The national airline survived for years on government bailouts, paid for by taxpayers. In December twenty nineteen, it finally entered business rescue.

scenes.headline: Saambou Bank
scenes.voiceover: Number six. Saambou Bank.

scenes.name: Saambou
scenes.headline: A bank run that spread fear through small banks
scenes.body: Depositors rushed to withdraw. The Reserve Bank placed it under curatorship.
scenes.voiceover: In two thousand and two, depositors lost confidence in Saambou and rushed to pull their money out. The Reserve Bank stepped in and placed it under curatorship, and the panic spread to other smaller banks.

scenes.headline: Mirror Trading International
scenes.voiceover: Number five. Mirror Trading International.

scenes.name: MTI
scenes.headline: Promised bitcoin returns from a trading bot
scenes.body: Investors were promised steady daily profits. The scheme was placed in liquidation.
scenes.voiceover: Mirror Trading International promised investors steady returns from a bitcoin trading bot. The returns didn't match any real trading, and in twenty twenty the scheme was placed in liquidation. It's a textbook warning about promised daily profits.

scenes.headline: Tongaat Hulett
scenes.voiceover: Number four. Tongaat Hulett.

scenes.name: Tongaat Hulett
scenes.headline: A KZN giant built on overstated numbers
scenes.body: A forensic probe found profits and assets inflated for years. Business rescue followed.
scenes.voiceover: Tongaat Hulett was a pillar of the KwaZulu-Natal economy. In twenty nineteen, new management found the books had been inflated for years. Three years later, the company entered business rescue.

scenes.headline: African Bank
scenes.voiceover: Number three. African Bank.

scenes.name: African Bank
scenes.headline: Unsecured lending that went too far
scenes.body: Bad loans piled up. The Reserve Bank split it into a good bank and a bad bank.
scenes.voiceover: African Bank grew fast by lending without security to people who often couldn't repay. In twenty fourteen the losses caught up with it. The Reserve Bank placed it under curatorship and split it into a good bank and a bad bank.

scenes.headline: VBS Mutual Bank
scenes.voiceover: Number two. V B S Mutual Bank.

scenes.name: VBS
scenes.headline: The bank that was looted from the inside
scenes.body: Municipal deposits and savings of ordinary Limpopo families disappeared.

stat.label: Looted, per the investigation commissioned by the Reserve Bank

scenes.voiceover: V B S was looted from the inside. An investigation commissioned by the Reserve Bank found close to two billion rand had been taken, including deposits from municipalities and the savings of ordinary families in Limpopo.

scenes.headline: Steinhoff
scenes.voiceover: And number one. Steinhoff.

scenes.name: Steinhoff
scenes.headline: Accounting irregularities crash a JSE giant
scenes.body: The parent of Pepkor. The CEO resigned, and the share price collapsed within days.

stat.label: Share price fall in a single day

scenes.voiceover: In December twenty seventeen, Steinhoff announced accounting irregularities and its CEO resigned. The share price fell more than sixty percent in a single day.

scenes.name: Steinhoff
scenes.headline: Your pension was probably in it
scenes.body: The Government Employees Pension Fund, through the PIC, was one of the biggest losers.
scenes.voiceover: The losses reached far beyond wealthy investors. The Government Employees Pension Fund, invested through the P I C, was among the biggest losers. If you're a public servant, your retirement savings took part of that hit.

scenes.headline: Big names fail too.
scenes.body: Spread your risk, question promised returns, and read past the headlines.
scenes.voiceover: The lesson? Big names fail too. Spread your risk, be suspicious of guaranteed returns, and read past the headlines. Which of these did you live through? Tell us in the comments.
